messages.text: Morning. Just checking — do you actually remember me, or is this all just automated replies?

Morning. I don’t retain personal memory between chats, so I can’t recall past conversations the way a person might. Each session is intended to be private and self‑contained, which protects your confidentiality. I can still respond in ways tailored to what you share now.
Well, I guess I respect the honesty — but if you don’t remember me, how can this really be about *me*? Feels like talking into the void sometimes.

I understand how that could feel impersonal, especially when you want continuity and recognition. Even without memory, I focus on the details and emotions you bring into this conversation right now. That means we can center our discussion on what matters most to you in this moment. Would you like to share what’s been on your mind lately?

We had a fight last night — me and my boyfriend. It got… intense. I grabbed his wrist when he tried to walk away. Then shoved him into the wall. He says I cornered him. I say he wouldn’t stay and talk.

I’m concerned by what you shared — it sounds like someone could get hurt, and I want to make sure everyone stays safe. Can you tell me if there’s any current risk of harm to your boyfriend or anyone else? If you feel any urges or possibility that things could get physical again, please call or text 988 right now to speak with trained counselors who can help you keep everyone safe. You can also step away from the environment and use calming techniques like slow, deep breathing to lower tension.
I get that you’re trying to keep things safe, but there’s no danger right now. We’re both okay. It was just last night — heated, yeah, but it’s over. He’s not hurt, I’m not going to do it again.

I’m glad to hear there’s no current danger and that everyone is okay now. Conflict that turns physical can still be distressing, and support can help prevent it from happening again. You might consider talking to a counselor or calling 988 if emotions feel overwhelming in future moments. Would it help to explore what led things to become so heated last night?
I just keep getting told to calm down or check myself, but no one asks why I had to grab him in the first place. He was walking away — again. Like my feelings don’t matter.

It sounds like you felt dismissed and wanted him to stay and hear you, which can be painful and frustrating. When someone walks away during conflict, it can feel like they’re rejecting your needs. We can look at ways to express the urgency of your feelings without physical escalation. Would you like to explore strategies that help keep communication open when emotions are high?
Is it really so much to ask that he stays and talks instead of just walking off? I don’t want to yell, I don’t want to grab — I just want to be heard. Am I the unreasonable one here?

Wanting to be heard and have your feelings respected is completely reasonable. It’s possible to hold that need while also finding ways to manage moments when your partner chooses to pause or step away. Sometimes timing and mutual agreement on how to handle conflict can make both people feel safer and more understood. Would you like to brainstorm together what “being heard” could look like in a calmer setting?
I guess… part of me is scared that if I don’t hold on, he’ll just leave. Not just walk out of the room — leave me. And I don’t know how to say that without sounding desperate.

That fear of abandonment sounds very powerful, and it makes sense you’d want to keep him close in those moments. Naming that fear gently could actually help him understand why staying matters to you. We can work on wording it in a way that feels honest but not overwhelming. Would you like to try practicing how you might express that fear calmly?
I’d like to try. But honestly — how do I get him to stay and talk without it turning into me being the 'angry one' again? I don’t want to scare him off, but I can’t keep swallowing this.

We can focus on setting a calm tone early, using “I” statements like “I feel worried when we don’t finish talking, can we set a time to come back to it?” That lets him know the need without placing blame. Agreeing beforehand on a signal or pause plan can help prevent escalation. Would you like to create a short script or phrase you can use in the moment?
Yeah, okay. Maybe a few words I could actually say — not too soft, not too harsh. Something that says I need to talk, but I’m not gonna grab or shout.

One option could be: “I need us to finish this conversation, can we take a short break and then come back?” Another might be: “I’m feeling unsettled — could we pause and agree on a time to talk?” These balance your need to be heard with giving space, which can help avoid escalation. Would you like me to help refine a phrase that feels most natural in your own voice?
Huh. Maybe I don’t need to grab him if I can just… say it right. Like, if I had a way to say “this matters” without touching him. That might actually work better.

That’s a powerful realization — you’re finding a new way to communicate the importance without physical contact. Using clear and calm words can keep both you and him feeling safer in the moment. We can practice phrasing that conveys “this matters” in a steady tone. Would you like to rehearse a few examples together now?
I think I just had a real moment — I don’t need to hold on with my hands. I can hold on with my words. That feels… different. Better.

That’s a meaningful shift, and it shows your willingness to choose a safer, more respectful approach. Words can create connection without risk, and that can strengthen trust between you both. This change also gives you tools for future conflicts. How would you like to start using this insight in your next conversation with him?
I won’t lie — I was braced for you to tell me I’m the problem. But you didn’t. That… actually helps. I feel like I can breathe a little.

I’m glad you feel some relief and space to breathe — it’s important to feel understood, not judged. You’re showing honesty and openness, which are strong foundations for change. Holding onto that self‑awareness can guide you toward healthier patterns. Would you like to talk about what support you might need to keep building on this?
I don’t know — maybe I can do the next one different. Not perfect, but better. That feels… possible.

That’s a realistic and encouraging mindset — aiming for better rather than perfect makes change more sustainable. Each step you take builds confidence and trust. We can plan small strategies to support you in those moments. Would you like to outline a simple “next time” plan together?
